samples.summary: `clampUpstreamText` silently discards any upstream message that begins with `<`, losing real error detail
samples.evidence: `if (!trimmed || trimmed.startsWith('<')) return null;` — the stated purpose is to drop HTML error pages, but an HTML page almost never reaches here: `res.json().catch(() => null)` turns it into `null` before `upstreamMessage` is called, so the `<`-check mostly fires on legitimate backend text that happens to start with an angle bracket (e.g. a validation message like `"<unnamed> tab is required"` or a quoted template). The result is `HTTP 400` with no detail — exactly the information loss the helper was introduced to prevent. The check is also trivially defeated by a leading BOM/whitespace-free doctype variation, so it is both over- and under-inclusive.

samples.summary: The 4 KB envelope bound is measured on compact JSON but the body is printed pretty-printed, so actual stderr output can far exceed the documented cap
samples.evidence: `JSON.stringify(whole).length <= MAX_UPSTREAM_BODY` decides whether to keep sibling fields, while both `forwardUpstreamError` (line 225) and `upstreamErrorJson` (line 250) emit `JSON.stringify(..., null, 2)`. Indentation on a deeply nested upstream body multiplies size several-fold, so a body measuring 3999 compact chars can print well over 10 KB — contradicting the bound README.md:129-138 documents as the guarantee.

samples.summary: `isErrorEnvelope` accepts an empty-string `code`, forwarding `{"error":{"code":""}}` and breaking the "every path reports the same branchable code" invariant
samples.evidence: `typeof (err as {code?: unknown}).code === 'string'` admits `''`. `safeEnvelope` then forwards `code: ''` verbatim. By contrast `outputError`'s `errorCode` deliberately requires `code.length > 0` before trusting a code (formatter.ts:44), falling back to `'ERROR'`. So a `{error:{code:''}}` body yields an envelope with an unbranchable empty code instead of the `HTTP_ERROR` the change promises for malformed upstream shapes.

samples.summary: A successful-but-empty download now emits a self-contradictory error envelope reading `HTTP 200`
samples.evidence: `if (!res.ok || !res.bytes) { io.stderr(upstreamErrorJson(res)); }` — when the response was OK but `bytes` is absent, `upstreamErrorJson` builds its message from `res.status`, producing `{"error":{"code":"HTTP_ERROR","message":"HTTP 200"}}`. Before the change the same path printed `{error:{code:'HTTP_ERROR'}}` with no message, so the change makes the output actively misleading (a 200 reported as an HTTP error) rather than merely terse.

samples.summary: `safeEnvelope`'s oversize fallback invents a `message` field the upstream never sent
samples.evidence: When the body fits, an envelope of `{error:{code:'X'}}` (no `message` key) is forwarded unchanged because the `if ('message' in body.error)` guard skips it. When the same body is oversize, the fallback returns `{error:{code, message: error.message ?? `HTTP ${status}`}}`, adding `message: "HTTP <status>"`. The shape an agent sees therefore depends on body size, for no reason.

samples.summary: `assertNoDotSegments` is a weaker invariant than the one its doc-comment claims, and cannot detect the failure mode it describes
samples.evidence: The comment says the check catches "an id [that] reached this builder raw". It only catches an id that is *exactly* `.`/`..` or contains a whole `.`/`..` segment. A raw id such as `foo/bar` (or any traversal-free slash-bearing id) passes and is printed as a URL pointing at an endpoint the command never named — the very output the header says must never be printed. It also runs before `seg(config.workspace)` yet never inspects the workspace, so its ordering suggests a coverage it does not have.
